extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters and TV creators pitching a television series to producers, networks, or streamers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating and delivering a TV show pitch document and verbal pitch (logline, one-sheet, show bible, pilot script, sizzle reel) aimed at getting a series into development with networks or streaming platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional hook
rubrics_metrics.description: The emotional hook is what draws your audience in. Give your story a strong emotional foundation and let the emotional core of your television show shine through.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the pitch personal and universal by appealing to emotions; connect the hook to main characters, their arcs and the show’s themes (examples: love, acceptance, forgiveness, trust, greed, redemption). In verbal pitches you can use your personal connection; in written documents evoke feelings through the prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logline
rubrics_metrics.description: The logline encapsulates the core concept of your TV show and summarizes the story in one or two sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answer: What is happening and to whom? Where and when does this take place? What is unique or why it stands apart? What is the emotional hook? Optionally include genre and format as prefixes (e.g., 'hour-long sci-fi mystery comedy-drama'). Example provided: Stranger Things logline that conveys who/what/where/when and emotional stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-sheet contents
rubrics_metrics.description: A one-sheet is a single-page condensed pitch used as a handout or calling card for your project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include contact information (name, phone, email), title, logline, genre and format, a short synopsis (one to three paragraphs or 8–12 lines), and additional info (biography, awards, showreel/sizzle reel link, or rights notes). It may be printed double-sided and should help executives remember the core idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series bible / show summary
rubrics_metrics.description: The series bible is a document giving essential details to bring newcomers up to speed and serving as marketing material for a pitch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address: Who are the main characters and what makes them/world unique? Why will the audience care? What choices do characters make and why? Why are you telling this story and why you? What will viewers take away? What is the tone, look and feel and how does it compare to other shows? Include title and logline, a series/season synopsis, main character descriptions, a TV pilot breakdown, and an outlook for future episodes/seasons (how many seasons/episodes, episode loglines or brief breakdowns). Keep it succinct; for short pitches 2–3 sentences per episode is enough.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pilot script inclusion and quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a completed pilot script as part of the pitch to demonstrate screenwriting skills, tone, character voice and how the concept translates to a real episode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pilot should allow decision-makers to evaluate writing style and visualize characters; it should 'stand on its own' and be able to win readers without other materials. A spec pilot can serve as proof of concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format and runtime clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the format details of your show clear (e.g., sitcom, docu-series, unscripted, half-hour, hour-long, horizontal/vertical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Executives categorize and compare projects; explicitly state genre and format in the logline/one-sheet/bible so networks can slot the show into their programming needs. Lack of clear format details reduces chances with platforms like Netflix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Future development / long-term plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide an outlook on the future development of the show, including how the series and characters will evolve beyond the pilot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include season arcs, number of anticipated seasons/episodes, episode loglines or short synopses for future episodes, and demonstrate long-term planning (completed character arcs or several-season plans when possible). This signals that you have thought through the series' trajectory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness and appropriate length
rubrics_metrics.description: Be succinct across materials—keep bibles and synopses focused and avoid unnecessary length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit the number of pages in the bible; use short episode descriptions (2–3 sentences) for pitch bibles. In meetings, keep verbal pitches brief—don’t narrate the document or deliver a play-by-play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know and target your audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Tailor the pitch to who you're selling to (production companies, executive producers, networks, streaming platforms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that execs 'think in categories' and may want buzzwords; adapt wording and emphasis to the buyer's brand and needs (e.g., HBO vs. Netflix vs. cable). Use comparisons to existing shows when helpful to categorise tone and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation style: brevity and delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Pitch delivery should be concise, confident, and engaging—avoid reading or overlong presentations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show personal connection and emotional hook, succinctly cover main characters and storyline, and leave the audience wanting more. Time your pitch and avoid filler; keep it conversational rather than sounding memorised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidence and author-as-teller
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate that you are the right person to tell the story and speak passionately about your project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin and end on the theme, explain why you relate to the story, and use passion to sell the big picture. Treat a pitch meeting as a two-way conversation—ask the execs questions to learn fit and show engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice and preparedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Rehearse your pitch to eliminate pauses, filler expressions, and timing issues while remaining conversational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memorize enough to avoid stumbles but avoid sounding rote; anticipate likely questions and prepare answers so you don't 'choke' when details are requested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility and collaborative willingness
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicate openness to development changes, collaboration with writers' rooms, and adjustments to align with network needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be ready to adapt runtime, season structure, or casting suggestions; avoid amateurish casting demands but you can invite casting suggestions. Expressing flexibility can smooth development discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sizzle reel use
rubrics_metrics.description: A sizzle reel is a short (3–5 minute) video showcasing your previous work and the show's tone, story, and style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use it to clearly present your show's core concept, narrative approach and main characters. It is not a trailer or promotional video; target it to decision-makers and either show it during the presentation or include a link in the pitch materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-sheet and bible formatting repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeat key identifiers (title and logline) and present information in easy-to-remember formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeat title/logline across one-sheet and bible; structure materials so readers can quickly find contact, logline, genre, synopsis and links. Treat the one-sheet as the executive's takeaway/flyer for recall.
